projects.title: Remote Work
projects.subtitle: Managerial WFH, wage discount and firm performance

profile.researchQuestion: What is the economic value of remote work for employees and firms, and how does it vary with the level of the corporate hierarchy at which it is adopted? In particular, do managers accept lower pay in return for flexibility, and does that choice entail costs or benefits for the firm?
profile.contribution: The draft combines individual compensation and firm outcomes to distinguish a potential compensating wage differential from worker selection and the organizational costs of working from home (WFH). Its distinctive contribution is measuring WFH across three hierarchical levels using Finnish administrative records, rather than treating it as a uniform firm characteristic. The connection between managers' wage discount and value added or retention remains interpretive rather than definitive causal evidence.
profile.methodology: Finnish administrative data for 2018–2023 linking a tax-return-based measure of WFH to employment histories, compensation, and company accounts: approximately 1.15 million worker-year and 49,000 firm-year observations in the November draft. An event study of job transitions within comparable occupations uses worker, origin firm × year, and destination firm × year fixed effects; firm panels examine ROA, value added per employee, and retention. Additional tests interact pre-pandemic teleworkability with the post-pandemic period; IV estimates require cautious interpretation.
profile.mainFindings: In the November draft, managers moving into jobs with WFH experience a roughly 3% wage decrease, an effect not found as robustly at other hierarchical levels. Overall WFH is not significantly related to ROA, whereas managerial WFH penetration is positively associated with ROA, value added per employee, and retention. The paper reports an association of approximately +0.16 ROA percentage points for a 10-percentage-point increase in managerial WFH. These are evolving draft findings, not established causal effects; productivity and IV results still require caution.

snapshot.progress: The team reviewed refined conference tables, including heterogeneity by parental status and commuting distance and summary statistics matched to the regression samples. Targeted manuscript revisions remain before conference submission.
snapshot.issue: Clarify the economic interpretation of managerial WFH without overclaiming supervisory-demand mechanisms; verify submission cutoffs and time zones.
snapshot.nextAction: Emanuele to revise the abstract and results narrative by November 14; Aleksi to add supervisory-demands framing by November 14; Matteo to finalize the manuscript and submit to WFA, FRS and Edinburgh on November 18, subject to verified deadlines.
snapshot.milestone: Conference-ready draft targeted by November 17; WFA, FRS and Edinburgh submissions targeted November 18. Code review, selected external feedback and an updated SSRN version planned for December.

projects.title: Neobrokers
projects.subtitle: Behavioral biases in digital vs traditional brokerage

profile.researchQuestion: Does the disposition effect—and investors' propensity to sell positions at gains or losses—differ between digital and traditional brokers for the same investor? Does behavior change when investors migrate between channels, compared with investors who continue to use both?
profile.contribution: A descriptive within-investor comparison of digital and traditional platforms, focusing on multihoming investors and distinguishing switchers from stayers. The potential contribution is to document how behavioral bias, sale timing, and subsequent outcomes covary with the channel. A causal effect of the digital interface has not yet been identified.
profile.methodology: Transactions and positions for the same investors across digital and traditional intermediaries. Measures of the disposition effect (PGR/PLR and propensity to sell), FIFO-based cost basis reconstruction, and price-completeness checks. Proposed specifications at the investor × security × platform × month level; switcher/stayer comparisons among multihoming investors, controlling for portfolio composition, liquidity needs, and transfers. The sample and identification strategy are still being refined.
profile.mainFindings: The preliminary October 8 report shows a smaller disposition effect on digital platforms (5.38 versus 6.08 percentage points on traditional platforms). Lorenzo also reports preliminary findings consistent with a lower bias following switching. The difference is descriptive: platform selection, security migration, forced sales, and liquidity needs may affect the estimates. The team decided to develop the storyline and core figures before claiming causal identification.

snapshot.progress: The disposition-effect analyses have progressed. Lorenzo proposes comparing switchers and stayers in the multihoming sample and reports preliminary evidence more consistent with lower disposition effects after a switch. The team agreed to move from exploratory analyses to a descriptive paper structure.
snapshot.issue: Structural selection issues persist in account and position choices, migration, and liquidity needs; fixed effects and alternative specifications do not automatically eliminate them. Do not claim causality or a top-journal contribution unsupported by the research design.
snapshot.nextAction: Lorenzo to draft an introduction outline (what is known, what is missing, why it matters) and select the sequence of figures and tables for discussion at the next meeting.

projects.title: Bankruptcy
projects.subtitle: Equity Holders, Court Shopping, and Bankruptcy Outcomes
projects.coauthors: Nicoletta Marinelli · Rafael Almeida da Matta · Wilson Pereira

profile.researchQuestion: Do sophisticated investors, including hedge funds, accumulate equity stakes in firms approaching Chapter 11, and how are those positions related to their roles as creditors, restructuring negotiations, and claim outcomes? To what extent do equity and debt positions overlap before and during bankruptcy proceedings?
profile.contribution: The proposed research design links pre-filing equity positions to debt positions and restructuring roles, distinguishing candidate explanations such as option value, hold-up, productive activism, and decoupling. Its value will depend on identifying beneficial owners and establishing novelty relative to distressed-investing, Chapter 11, and court-shopping research. No mechanism has yet been demonstrated.
profile.methodology: A pilot of ten Chapter 11 cases selected for differences in hedge-fund equity ownership (five above 50%, five at or below 10%) and LSEG coverage. Manually reconstruct pre-filing equity positions, beneficial debt ownership, RSA/DIP financing, and claim treatment. Potential sources include LSEG, the Florida-UCLA-LoPucki database, Kroll documents, court filings, SEC, DealScan, and Orbis, to be checked case by case. Any expansion to regression analyses depends on successful matching.
profile.mainFindings: There are no conclusive findings on the main research question yet. In a separate exploratory exercise involving 57 cases reconstructed from Kroll records, Nicoletta reports equity cancellation in 42 (about 74%), sometimes with contingent recovery for former shareholders. This illustrates why post-filing ownership is difficult to use, but is not evidence of equity–debt overlap or causality in hedge-fund behavior. The latest documented activity is the selection of ten pilot cases.

projects.title: Sherry
projects.subtitle: Investor Days: prepared remarks, Q&A and multimodal disclosure

profile.researchQuestion: Do the visual, vocal, and textual signals communicated by executives during Investor Days—particularly the contrast between prepared remarks and Q&A—convey economically relevant information beyond spoken words? Who attends these events, how do fund positions change, and how are Investor Days associated with subsequent seasoned equity offerings (SEOs)?
profile.contribution: A three-study research program outlined in the revised July 2026 PhD presentation: (1) construction and validation of a cross-modal inconsistency measure in webcasts; (2) investor attendance and portfolio reallocation; and (3) the frequency and underpricing of subsequent SEOs following Investor Days. The novelty of the measure and its links to economic outcomes are hypotheses and intended contributions, not yet established results.
profile.methodology: The current sample reported by Xinyue comprises 233 validated webcasts, approximately 647 hours. The proposed pipeline identifies speakers and segments, extracts visual, vocal, and verbal representations, and measures inconsistency using a leave-one-modality-out approach; scripted remarks are compared with Q&A within speaker and event. Potential extensions include FactSet participant tagging, 13F/CRSP mutual-fund data for active portfolio-weight changes, expected-return measures, and subsequent SEOs. Validity, coverage, and selection checks are still needed.
profile.mainFindings: Xinyue's preliminary analyses indicate multimodal differences between prepared remarks and Q&A and a strong common component in executives' movements (approximately 68–88% in some measures), leaving within-event variation to interpret. Neither independent information content of the measure nor effects on fund holdings, returns, or SEO underpricing have been demonstrated. An Investor Relations interview transcript arrived November 6 but its contents had not yet been analyzed at this snapshot.

snapshot.progress: 233 validated webcasts, approximately 647 hours; preliminary multimodal differences between prepared remarks and Q&A. On November 6, Xinyue shared a Brown-Forman IR interview transcript, and Emanuele replied with guidance for further qualitative interviews.
snapshot.issue: Separate natural contextual variation from informative signals; validate the measures.
snapshot.nextAction: Xinyue to validate the multimodal measures, connect them to fund holdings and economic outcomes, and conduct follow-up qualitative IR interviews on invitation decisions and investor relationships. Consider a structured questionnaire only after further interviews.

projects.title: Brand Gender
projects.subtitle: Beyond the Ticker — investor responses to brand gender
projects.coauthors: Nicoletta Marinelli · Otto Randl · Giorgia Simion

profile.researchQuestion: Does a firm's symbolically feminine or masculine representation in brand imagery affect fund managers' portfolio decisions? In particular, do male managers underweight firms with more feminine imagery, and does this reflect selective attention rather than economic fundamentals or familiarity with the products?
profile.contribution: 'Beyond the Ticker' extends research on financial gender biases from individuals' characteristics to firms' gendered symbolic identities, introducing an image-based GenderScore. The proposed rational-inattention explanation faces a JFQA referee's criticism that the design does not adequately separate symbolic imagery from fundamentals and alternative explanations; its causal contribution therefore remains contested.
profile.methodology: Image recognition on more than 300,000 images linked to 135 brands measures the share of people perceived as women and constructs GenderScore. These measures are linked to portfolios of actively managed U.S. equity mutual funds with a single portfolio manager over 2008–2021. The analysis examines stock inclusion and weights, manager turnover, trading intensity, and reactions to news or analyst recommendations, with controls and alternative checks. An editorial critique called for better handling of confounders, potentially including stock × quarter fixed effects.
profile.mainFindings: The manuscript reports that male managers are less likely to hold firms with more feminine imagery, without a symmetric aversion by female managers toward more masculine firms. Manager turnover, trading, and reactions to news are consistent with differential attention; conditional on trading, no performance penalties emerge. The authors propose rational inattention, but the evidence does not definitively distinguish imagery, familiarity, and fundamentals. The paper was under review at the Journal of Corporate Finance at the October 25, 2026 check.

projects.title: Favoritism in Academia
projects.subtitle: Reviewer connections, evaluation mechanisms and allocation

profile.researchQuestion: Are professional ties among researchers—through institutional affiliations, coauthorship, and academic communities—associated with research-evaluation outcomes and potential favoritism? Can genuine links between evaluators and authors be distinguished from merely belonging to the same university or discipline?
profile.contribution: The contribution remains to be defined: construct observable measures of academic proximity and connection to study evaluation decisions, distinguishing social networks, scientific quality, and institutional structures. A connection does not establish favoritism; a sample of evaluation decisions and a credible empirical design will be needed to interpret estimated coefficients.
profile.methodology: Luca reconstructed affiliation and coauthorship networks (12,615 individuals, 25,549 coauthorship ties, and 67 communities according to the project materials). He tested a community-detection algorithm yielding groups that largely overlap with universities. Next steps: verify the code, merge network variables into the evaluation dataset, and formulate regressions with appropriate controls. The final specification and evaluation dataset have not yet been verified.
profile.mainFindings: The documented result so far is largely infrastructural: coauthorship networks form clusters that substantially overlap with academic institutions. No empirical evidence has yet been produced or verified on the effects of author–evaluator ties or favoritism. Delivery of the dataset containing network variables remains pending.

projects.title: Minor Trading
projects.subtitle: Delegated trading for minors and within-family transmission

profile.researchQuestion: How do parents invest on behalf of underage children, how similar are investment decisions between parents and children or among siblings, and what changes when a child turns 18? Can parental preferences and sophistication be distinguished from young investors' independent behavior?
profile.contribution: The potential novelty is using linked family data on parents, children's accounts, and siblings to study delegated investing and the transition to adulthood. Several mechanisms have been considered (portfolio risk, trading, taxation, and attention to news), but the main contribution and the decision to develop a paper have not yet been settled.
profile.methodology: Transaction data linking decision-makers, parents, and children, including family units with one parent and two siblings, one of whom turns 18. Proposed exploratory analyses examine portfolio similarity, turnover, and concentration; within-parent and sibling comparisons; event studies around age 18; and potentially tax-related round trips. Errors in birth year and decision-maker identifiers were cleaned, but the granularity of demographic data and a short post-18 period constrain the tests.
profile.mainFindings: Descriptive statistics and exploratory analyses are available, but no replicated, central scientific finding ready for publication has emerged. Lorenzo stabilized the sample during summer 2026 and proposed testable hypotheses, including risk differences between parents' own and children's accounts and responses around news events. At the November 3 meeting, framing and priority relative to other projects remained unresolved.

snapshot.progress: At the November 3 meeting, Lorenzo confirmed having conducted exploratory analyses of minors' accounts during the summer, with preliminary data and results but no persuasive scientific framing yet. The project is less advanced than the disposition-effect work; the team proposed reviewing available evidence rather than making a final decision to proceed.
snapshot.issue: The scientific contribution and positioning remain undefined. The team needs to assess whether the existing analyses can support a coherent paper and whether to allocate resources to it rather than alternatives such as payment for order flow, as part of the project priorities to be agreed with Claudia and the team.
snapshot.nextAction: Lorenzo to revisit existing analyses and prepare the main figures and tables for a future discussion of the project's feasibility and storyline. The November 11 joint call was canceled; the follow-up with Lorenzo is expected next week, date to be confirmed. A separate planning discussion with Claudia was expected for November 16 (not confirmed).

projects.title: Author Journal Networks
projects.subtitle: Journal proximity, latent targeting demand and the economics of scholarly publishing

profile.researchQuestion: Can published outcomes and author–journal networks be used to infer researchers' propensities to publish in particular outlets and a measure of latent journal targeting demand, even without observing rejected submissions or the set of journals authors considered?
profile.contribution: The study proposes aggregating author-level predictions of publication outlets into a measure of latent targeting demand and examining journal competition, combining topical fit, prior publication choices, and networks. The economic meaning of the measure needs clarification: predicting the journal of publication does not directly identify submission flows, acceptance rates, or causal demand.
profile.methodology: Following initial Crossref collection and construction of author–journal networks, the current model (according to Raju's email) uses approximately 225,000 articles, 235,000 author identifiers, and 180 ABDC journals over 2010–2025. It combines research–outlet similarity, network proximity, past publications, and a journal's historical popularity, evaluating published destinations through predictive rankings. The November 5 draft attachment had not yet been examined in detail at this snapshot.
profile.mainFindings: Raju reports that, for journals an author had never previously used, the model places 43.7% of observed publication destinations within its top ten, versus 38.7% using similarity alone. He also reports relatively stable rankings that are strongly correlated with journal size. These figures come from his email and have not yet been verified against the manuscript; they do not directly measure submission demand.

snapshot.progress: Raju sent a draft following the experiments, describing the computational work as reasonably mature. His email outlines a publication-propensity model and an aggregate latent-targeting-demand measure.
snapshot.issue: The study does not observe unsuccessful submissions or journals considered ex ante, so the measure does not identify submission volumes or acceptance probabilities. Its link to journal choice, academic incentives, journal competition, and scholarly publishing economics needs strengthening. The correlation with journal size requires careful interpretation.
